en: The *Buddhabhāṣita-gaṇanāsūtra*, translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Faju of the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying in the East Garden, at the Deer Park in Śrāvastī.
At that time, several brahmins, having finished their midday meal, were walking about aimlessly when they came to where the Blessed One was.
Having arrived, they exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
Having exchanged greetings and offered words of comfort, he sat down to one side.
Once those several brahmins had sat down to one side, they addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"O Gautama!..."
"I wish to ask something; please listen to my question. "Ask, brahmin;
ask whatever you desire."
“O Gautama! This Deer Park Lecture Hall was constructed and completed in successive stages,
O Gautama!”
"Ānanda, when this Mṛgadāva lecture hall is first ascended by means of a flight of stairs, it is done in this way; likewise for the second, third, and fourth.
Gautama, in this manner, one ascends the Mṛgadāva lecture hall in successive order."
"Gotama! This elephant trainer teaches and trains in successive stages, namely by holding the hook in his hand. Gotama!"
This horse-rider trains in sequence and learns in sequence, meaning he has already been harnessed. O Gautama!
This kṣatriya likewise trains in sequence and learns in sequence, meaning he wields the bow and arrow.
"Gotama! This brahmin studies in successive stages and learns in successive stages; that is to say, he studies the poetic verses. Gotama!"
We study calculation; we maintain our lives by means of calculation.
If one calculates for a disciple, even for a small child, one counts them as one, two, three, two, three, or ten, or a hundred, or more.
"It is so, Gautama! We study calculation;
we subsist by means of calculation. We teach it in sequence and learn it in sequence—this is what we call studying calculation, Śramaṇa Gautama!"
"In this Dharma and Vinaya, by what instruction and what training can it be known?
"Moggallāna, if you were to speak in this way,
would you be speaking correctly?"
"Teaching in sequence, training in sequence, and practicing the teaching of the precepts—
Maudgalyāyana, if one were to speak thus, would that not be speaking in sequence?"
Regarding my Dharma and Vinaya, for what reason is it so, Maudgalyāyana?
Within my Dharma and Vinaya, there is a sequential instruction, a sequential practice of the precepts, and a sequential training.
"O Maudgalyāyana!
This bhikṣu is a beginner who has not long been ordained; he has not yet received instruction from the Tathāgata regarding this Dharma and Vinaya. O bhikṣu!"
He purifies his conduct through equal purity of bodily action; he purifies his conduct through equal purity of speech and mind. Moggallāna!
If a bhikkhu purifies his conduct through equal purity of bodily action and purifies his conduct through equal purity of speech and mind, he is guided by the Tathāgata, the Unsurpassed Charioteer.
"This bhikṣu, Maudgalyāyana, should dwell contemplating the body as the body internally, and so on, until he dwells contemplating feelings, the mind, and phenomena as phenomena. This bhikṣu,

dwelling thus in the contemplation of the body as the body internally, and so on, until dwelling in the contemplation of feelings, the mind, and phenomena as phenomena— he is guided by the Tathāgata, the Unsurpassed Charioteer."

“This bhikṣu should guard the doors of the sense faculties; he should protect his own mind and maintain mindfulness of the mind, practicing with diligent effort. When his eye sees forms, he should neither grasp at perceptions nor grasp at conceptualizations, for fear that they may become a condition for further increase.”
Guarding the faculty of the eye, one is free from shamelessness, greed, and a mind of sorrow; one does not dwell in unwholesome or evil states. Training therein, one guards the faculty of the eye.

Likewise for the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind: when the body and mind cognize dharmas, one should neither grasp at perceptions nor grasp at other perceptions, because of the influence of superior causes and conditions.
This faculty of mind is shameless, characterized by greed, sorrow, and dejection; unwholesome states do not abide within it. While training therein, one protects this faculty of mind.
This, Moggallāna!

If a bhikṣu, having fully mastered the doors of the sense faculties, guards his own mind so that it is free from defilement, guarding the mind with mindfulness; and while practicing equanimity and diligence together with mindfulness, when he sees forms with the eye, he neither grasps at perceptions nor grasps at other perceptions, because of the presence of superior conditions.
Possessing the faculty of the eye, he is free from shamelessness, greed, anxiety, and dejection; he does not abide in unwholesome or evil states. Training therein, he guards the faculty of the eye.

Likewise, regarding the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind that cognize phenomena, he does not grasp at perceptions. Training therein, he guards the faculty of the mind until he reaches it; thus the Tathāgata, the Unsurpassed Guide, governs him.

"This bhikṣu, having transcended [the past], should practice equanimity regarding what is to be done; having practiced it, whether bending or stretching, carrying the saṃghāṭī robe and bowl, whether walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, or remaining silent, he should maintain equanimity."
"O Maudgalyāyana!
If a bhikṣu has transcended what is past and proceeds toward the practice of equanimity, he is guided by the Tathāgata, the Unsurpassed Charioteer.

This bhikṣu, having understood the bedding and lying down, accepts it; whether in a quiet place, at the foot of a tree, in an empty and secluded spot, within a mountain cave, sitting in the open air on a grass mat, or among the woods and burial mounds—if he is in a quiet place, he spreads his saṃstaraṇa, sits cross-legged, straightens his body and sets his intention, with the mind foremost. He dwells having removed thoughts of greed and envy, free from ill will, and does not give rise to greed for the wealth of others, thinking, 'May another's property become mine. Thus he purifies the mind of greed."

In this way, having removed ill-will, sloth, torpor, restlessness, and shame; having eliminated doubt and greed, and being free from perversion, doubt, and all states of hesitation, he purifies the mind of uncertainty. Abandoning the five hindrances and the fetters that bind the mind, his wisdom is liberated from the weakness of sensual desire, and he attains and abides in the four dhyānas.
Thus it is, Maudgalyāyana!
A bhikṣu is liberated from sensual desire up to abiding in the fourth dhyāna.
Thus it is, Maudgalyāyana!
The Tathāgata brings great benefit to beginner bhikṣus by teaching them both doctrine and practice.
"Maudgalyāyana, those elder bhikṣus who are recognized by kings, who dwell without indolence and practice the holy life, are guided by the Tathāgata, the unsurpassed leader."
That is to say, they reach the ultimate exhaustion of all taints; all disciples of the Śramaṇa Gautama, being thus instructed and thus taught, reach the ultimate exhaustion and draw near to Nirvāṇa.
"Maugandika! It is not exclusively one way, nor is it exclusively the other.
"Gautama! [Maudgalyāyana replied.]
For what cause and for what reason do you say that there is nirvāṇa and a path to seek nirvāṇa?
Śramaṇa Gautama!
You dwell in a state capable of instruction; some bhikṣus you instruct and teach in such a way that they reach the ultimate end and are directed toward the ultimate nirvāṇa, while others do not.
"Therefore, Maudgalyāyana, I shall question you in return; answer as you see fit.
What do you think, Maudgalyāyana?"
"Do you know well the road back to Rājagṛha?
"Indeed, Gautama!
I know well the road back to Rājagṛha."
"Suppose someone were to come, wishing to go to Rājagṛha to reach the king's presence; they would come to you and say:
'The Brahmin Maudgalyāyana is well-acquainted with the number of roads leading to Rājagṛha. I wish to go to Rājagṛha to reach the king's presence and ask for directions.'"
"You should speak thus:

'You should proceed rightly by this path; having proceeded rightly, you will reach that village; having reached that village, you will arrive at that place; therefore, you shall reach Rājagṛha in due course.'"

That is to say, in Rājagṛha, there is the joy of the gardens, the joy of the groves, the joy of the grounds, the joy of the ponds, and the cool, refreshing flow of the rivers—a state of peace and happiness.
‘You should know this; you should see this.
He accepts your instruction and receives it accordingly; having received the instruction, he proceeds directly toward that goal by means of that path.
Having proceeded directly to that goal, he instead takes a wrong path and walks away from it.
Regarding that pleasure grove in Rājagṛha—its delightful and secure bliss—he neither knows it nor sees it.
Suppose someone were to come to you, having business with the king and intending to go to Rājagṛha, and were to say this:
"The brahmin Moggallāna well knows the roads to Rājagṛha; I wish to go to Rājagṛha and now ask you for the way."
"You should speak thus:
'By means of this path, go straight on; having gone straight on, you will reach that village; having reached that village, you will arrive at that place.'"
"He proceeded in due order to Rājagṛha; regarding that Rājagṛha, he knew and saw it as a place of delightful and secure happiness.
Thus, Moggallāna!
For what cause and for what reason does that Rājagṛha exist? For what cause and for what reason do the roads to Rājagṛha exist?

You remain there to instruct, and that first person, having received your instruction, yet does not accept it; he takes a wrong path and departs in the opposite direction, saying, "In Rājagṛha, the park grounds are delightful and lead to peace and happiness," yet he neither knows nor sees this.

Following those instructions and receiving that teaching, the two men took up the path and proceeded in due order to Rājagṛha. Regarding Rājagṛha, they perceived it as a delightful parkland, reaching a state of peace, bliss, and tranquility; thus they came to know it and they came to see it.
“O Gautama! What am I to do?

There is Rājagṛha, and there are roads leading to Rājagṛha. I remain here to instruct them, yet those who first come do not accept the instruction as taught; they take the wrong path and go back, saying that the pleasure-groves of Rājagṛha are delightful and bring peace and happiness. Yet they neither know nor see them.”

Those two men, following the instructions as taught and taking up that path, proceeded in due order to Rājagṛha; they said that in Rājagṛha there were delightful parks leading to peace and happiness, and they would come to know and see them.
"Thus it is, Moggallāna! What could I possibly do?
There is that Nirvāṇa, and there is the path to Nirvāṇa; I abide in teaching, and when I instruct and direct a certain bhikṣu in such a way, he reaches the ultimate end and draws near to Nirvāṇa."
Or perhaps one is not so. This, Moggallāna,
refers to that bhikkhu who receives instruction therein, and who receives teaching and guidance within the assembly of the Blessed One, leading ultimately to the exhaustion of all taints.
“Already surpassed, Gautama!
Already surpassed, Gautama!
It is just as if, Gautama!”

In an excellent location there was a grove of *sāla* trees. The one who tended that *sāla* grove practiced his duties diligently and without slackening. By his own strength, he would go to the roots of those *sāla* trees; from time to time he would dig them up and examine them. He would cast manure into the soil, water it, and if anything was not full, he would fill it with earth. If there were weeds at the edges, he would pull them out and discard them. If there were creeping vines—withered, evil, crooked, and not straight—he would pull them all out and discard them, meaning he would remove whatever was newly sprouted. He would cause what was initially grown to grow very large, tending it with water according to the season, casting manure into the soil, and watering it.
"So it is, Gautama!
This beautiful grove of sāla trees will, in time, grow to be exceedingly vast.
So it is, Gautama!"

That is to say, such a person is flatterer and deceitful, acting like a phantom; they lack faith, are indolent, and their will is distracted and unstable. Their wisdom is corrupt, their mind is disordered, and their faculties are unsettled. They are not diligent in their observance of precepts and do not thoroughly discern the conduct of a śramaṇa.
"Śramaṇa Gautama!
I do not stay overnight with him, nor do I dwell together with such a person. Why is that?"
"Gotama! It is so;
such a person is one who destroys the holy life.

Gotama, that person is said to be without flattery and without crooked intent; he practices with faith and diligence, his mind constantly abides in concentration and wisdom, he follows the training of reverence and morality, and he extensively discerns the conduct of a śramaṇa."
"Śramaṇa Gautama!
You are one who is unattached; it is fitting that you should dwell together with such a person as this. Why is that?"
"Gotama! Such a person as this is one who is in accordance with the Dharma and pure among those who lead the holy life.
It is just so, Gotama!"
Among all fragrant roots, the kāra is the most excellent.
Why is this so, Gautama?
"Among those Kāla trees, Gautama, the Sāl-scented variety is the foremost,
just as red sandalwood is the foremost among all fragrant woods. Why is that?"
Gautama! Among all the *sāla* fragrances, red sandalwood is preeminent.
It is just so, Gautama!
Among all flowers that grow in water, the blue utpala is foremost.
Why is this so, Gautama?
Among all water flowers, the blue lotus (*utpala*) is preeminent. Just so, Gautama!
Among all land flowers, the *sumana* and *bālisika* are preeminent.
Why is this so? Gautama!
Among all flowers on land, the pāṭali is preeminent.
"Just as, Gautama, among all worldly discourses, the discourse of the śramaṇa Gautama is the most excellent. Why is this so?"
The discourse of the Śramaṇa Gautama is able to encompass all heterodox teachings.
Therefore, World-Honored One,
I now take refuge in the Dharma and the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus.
"O World-Honored One!
I now take up the status of an upāsaka; from this day forth until the end of my life, I shall abstain from taking life. I now take refuge.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
The Brahmin Śreṇika, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and was glad.
This is the Sūtra on Śreṇika spoken by the Buddha.
